name: Nicarchus
bio: Nicarchus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 1st century AD.
This archive carries the 5 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book V: 38, 39, 40; Book VI: 31, 285).

poems.title: Book V, 38
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A fine and largely built woman attracts me, Similus, whether she be in her prime, or elderly. If she be young she will clasp me, if she be old and wrinkled, me fellabit.

poems.title: Book V, 39
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Must I not die? What care I if I go to Hades with gouty legs or in training for a race? I shall have many to carry me; so let me become lame, if I wish. As far as that goes, as you see, I am quite easy, and never miss a banquet.

poems.title: Book V, 40
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Don’t listen to your mother, Philumena; for once I am off and out of the town, pay no attention to those who make fun of us, but give them tit for tat, and try to be more successful than I was. Leave no stone unturned, make your own living, and write and tell me what pleasances you have visited. Try and behave with propriety. If you have anything over, pay the rent and get a coat for me. If you get with child, bring it to the birth, I entreat you. Don’t be troubled about that: when it grows up it will find out who its father was.

poems.title: Book VI, 31
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.note: Paton marks the attribution with a query.
poems.text: I nave offered this as a common gift to Pan the goattreader, to Dionysus the giver of good fruit, and to Demeter the Earth-goddess, and I beg from them fine flocks, good wine and to gather good grain from the ears.

poems.title: Book VI, 285
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.note: Paton marks the attribution with a query.
poems.text: Nicarete, who formerly was in the service of Athene’s shuttle, and stretched out many a warp on the loom, made in honour of Cypris a bonfire in front of her house of her work-basket and bobbins and her other gear, crying, “Away with ye, starving work of wretched women, that have power to waste away the bloom of youth.” Instead the girl chose garlands and the lyre, and a gay life spent in revel and festivity. “Cypris,” she said, “I will pay thee tithe of all my gains. Give me work and take from it thy due.”

poems.title: Book VII, 159
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Orpheus won the highest prize among mortals by his harp, Nestor by the skill of his sweet-phrased tongue, divine Homer, the learned in lore, by the art of his verse, but Telephanes, whose tomb this is, by the flute.

poems.title: Book IX, 330
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A. “I am goat-footed Pan, whom Simo put up by the clear waters of the spring.” B. “And why?” A. “I will tell thee. From the fountain drink as much as thou wilt, and take this hollow pitcher, too, and draw. But offer not the crystalline gifts of the Nymphs to thy feet to bathe them. Seest thou not my menacing form?” B. “Revered god—” A. “Thou shalt not speak another word, but shalt let me take my will of thee. Such is the custom of Pan. But if thou dost it! on purpose, having an inclination for the penalty, I know another trick. I will break thy head with my club.”

poems.title: Book IX, 576: On a Statue of Athena holding an Apple. Aphrodite speaks
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Trito-born maiden, why dost thou vex me now by grasping in thy hand my prize of which thou hast robbed me. Thou rememberest how formerly, amid the rocks of Ida, Paris pronounced me fairest, not thee. Thine are the spear and shield, but mine is the apple. For the apple that old war was surely enough.

poems.title: Book XI, 1
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: At the feast of Hermes, Aphrodisius, as he was carrying six choes of wine, stumbled and threw us into deep mourning. ‘“ Wine was the death even of the Centaurs.” Would it had been ours; but now it is it we have lost.

poems.title: Book XI, 7
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: No one, Charidemus, can constantly sleep with his own wife and take heart-felt pleasure in it. Our nature is so fond of titillation, such a luster after foreign flesh, that it persists in seeking the illusion of a strange caze.

poems.title: Book XI, 17
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Stephanus was poor and a gardener, but now having got on well and become rich, he has suddenly turned into Philostephanus, adding four fine letters to the original Stephanus, and in due time he will be Hippocratippiades or, owing to his extravagance, Dionysiopeganodorus. But in all the market he is still Stephanus.

poems.title: Book XI, 18
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Philaenis without conceiving bore a girl child to Heliodorus spontaneously, and when he was vexed at its being a girl she let six days pass and said she had borne a boy. So it is all over with Bubastis ; for if every woman is brought to bed like Philaenis, ' who will pay any attention to the goddess?

poems.title: Book XI, 71
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: NIconor was once in her prime, I admit that, but her prime was when Deucalion looked on the vast waters. Of those times we have no knowledge, but of her now we know that she should seek not a husband, but a tomb.

poems.title: Book XI, 73
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A handsome old woman (why deny it?) you know she was, when she was young; but then she asked for money while now she is ready to pay her mount. You will find her an artist, and when she has had something to drink then all the more you will have her submissive to whatever you want. For she drinks, if you consent, three or four pints, and then things are all topsy-turvy with her; she clings, she scratches, she plays the pathic; and if one gives her anything, she accepts, if not, the pleasure is her payment.

poems.title: Book XI, 74
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Turn out that stone-deaf old woman, Onesimus, for God’s sake, she is such a nuisance tome. If we tell her to bring soft cheeses (turot), she comes not with cheeses, but with fresh grains of wheat (purot). The other day I had a headache and asked her for rue (peganon) and she brought me an earthenware frying-pan (teganon) ; if I ask her for she brings me a rafter; if I say when I am hungry, “ Give me some greens ’”’ (lachanon), she at once brings a night-stool (lasanon). If I ask for vinegar (oxon), she brings me a bow (foxon), and if I ask for a bow, she brings vinegar ; in fact she does not comprehend a word I say. It would disgrace me to become a crier all for the sake of the old woman, and to get up at night and practise outside the town.

poems.title: Book XI, 82
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Charmus in Arcadia in the long race with five others came in (wonderful to say, but it is a fact) seventh. “As there were six,’ you will probably say, “how seventh?” A friend of his came in his overcoat calling out “Go it, Charmus,” so that thus he ran in seventh and if he had had five more friends, Zoilus, he would have come in twelfth.

poems.title: Book XI, 96
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: The birds of Stymphalus vexed not so the Arcadians, as those dead thrushes vexed me with their dry bones, very harpies, ten of them, a dry drachma’s-worth. Out on you, wretched creatures, true bats of the fields.

poems.title: Book XI, 110
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Three thin men were competing the other day about thinness, to see which of them would be adjudged the very thinnest. The one, Hermon, exhibited great skill and went through the eye of a needle holding the thread. But Demas coming out of a hole stopped at a spider’s web, and the spider spinning hung him from it. But Sosipater exclaimed, “ Give me the prize, for I lose it if I am seen, since I am nothing but air.”

poems.title: Book XI, 111
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Lean Diophantus once wishing to hang himself took a thread from a spider’s web and did so.

poems.title: Book XI, 112
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Before he anoints your eyes, Demostratus, say “ Adieu dear light,” so successful is Dion. Not only did he blind Olympicus, but through his treatment of him put out the eyes of the portrait of himself he had.

poems.title: Book XI, 113
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: The physician Marcus laid his hand yesterday on the stone Zeus, and though he is of stone and Zeus he is to be buried to-day.

poems.title: Book XI, 114
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: The astrologer Diophantus told Hermogenes the doctor that he had only nine months to live, and he, smiling, said, “ You understand what Saturn says will happen in nine months, but my treatment is more expeditious for you.”” Having said so he reached out his hand and only touched him, and Diophantus, trying to drive another to despair, himself gave his last gasp.

poems.title: Book XI, 115
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: If you have an enemy, Dionysius, call not down on him the curse of Isis or Harpocrates or of any god who blinds men, but call on Simon and you will see what a god’s power is and what Simon’s is.

poems.title: Book XI, 116
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Lord Caesar, as they tell, Eurystheus once sent down great Heracles to the house of Hades; but now Menophanes the physician has sent me. So let him be called Doctor Eurystheus and no longer Doctor Menophanes.

poems.title: Book XI, 124
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A. Stranger, what dost thou seek to know? B. Who are here in earth under these tombs? A. All those whom Zopyrus robbed of the sweet day-light, Damis, Aristoteles, Demetrius, Arcesilaus, Sostratus, and the next ones so far as Paraetonium. For with a wooden herald’s staff and counterfeit sandals,” like Hermes, he leads down his patients to Hell.

poems.title: Book XI, 162
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: One came to ask the prophet Olympicus if he should take ship for Rhodes and how to sail there safely. And the prophet said, “First have a new ship and don’t start in winter, but in summer. If you do this you will go there and back, unless a pirate catches you at sea.”’

poems.title: Book XI, 169
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Yesterday, Glaucus, Dinarchus the miser being about to hang himself, did not die, poor fellow, all for the sake of sixpence ; for the rope cost sixpence, but he tried to drive a hard bargain, seeking perhaps some other cheap death. This is the very height of wretched avarice, for a man to be dying, Glaucus, and not able to die, poor fellow, all for the sake of sixpence.

poems.title: Book XI, 170
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Philo the miser weeps not because he is dying, but because he paid thirty pounds for his coffin, Let him off this, and as there is room in it, put one of his many little children into it besides.

poems.title: Book XI, 186
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: The night-raven’s song bodes death, but when Demophilus sings the night-raven itself dies.

poems.title: Book XI, 241
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Your mouth and your breech, Theodorus, smell the same, so that it would be a famous task for men of science to distinguish them. You ought really to write on a label which is your mouth and which your breech, but now when you speak I think you break wind.

poems.title: Book XI, 242
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: I can’ tell whether Diodorus is yawning or has broken wind, for he has one breath above and below.

poems.title: Book XI, 243
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Onesimus went to the bath to bathe on the twelfth of the month Dystrus in the year of Antiphilus, leaving at home a child at the breast, whom when he has finished bathing he will find to be the father of two other children. . . . He writes us to say he will go again next year, for the bath-men promise to take off the heat then.

poems.title: Book XI, 251
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A stone-deaf man went to law with another stone-deaf man, and the judge was much deafer than the pair of them. One of them contended that the other owed him five months’ rent, and the other said that his opponent had ground corn at night. Says the judge, looking at them: “ Why are you quarrelling? She is your mother; you must both maintain her.”

poems.title: Book XI, 252
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: If you kiss me you hate me, and if you hate me you kiss me. But if you don’t hate me, dear friend, don’t kiss me!

poems.title: Book XI, 329
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Demonax, do not always turn down your eyes, nor indulge your tongue; the pig has a formidable thorn. And you live... and sleep in Phoenicia, and though not Semele’s son, art nourished by a thigh.

poems.title: Book XI, 330
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: I was invited yesterday, Demetrius, and came to supper to-day. Don’t find fault with me; you have a long staircase. I spent an age on it, and I should not have got safe up it to-day only I came up holding on to a donkey’s tail. You touch the stars: Zeus, it seems, when he ran away with Ganymede, went up with him by this route. But from here how long will it take you to reach Hades? You are not wanting in cleverness; you have hit on a trick for being immortal.

poems.title: Book XI, 331
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Philo had a boat called the “Saviour,” but in it perhaps not even Zeus himself can be saved. Its name only was Saviour, but the passengers sailed either close to land or to Persephone.

poems.title: Book XI, 332
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: Icanver the captain embarked us, it seems, on his twenty-oarer, not for a sail, but to bale her out. For the water in her is not little, but Poseidon seems to sail over in her to the opposite shore. It is the first time a ship with the dropsy has been seen. But I, at least, fear lest you may see what was once a long boat turn into our long home.

poems.title: Book XI, 395
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A r—r which cannot find an outlet kills many a man; a f—t also saves, sending forth its lisping music. Therefore if a f—t saves, and on the other hand kills, a f—t has the same power as kings.

poems.title: Book XI, 398
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: A man, by dyeing his head, destroyed the hair itself, and his head from being very hairy became all like an egg. The dyer attained this result, that no barber now ever cuts his hair be it white or dark.

poems.title: Book XI, 406
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: I see Nicon’s hooked nose, Menippus, and it is evident that he himself is not far off. Well, he will come; let us wait all the same, for at most he is not, I suppose, more than half a mile from his nose. But it, as you see, comes on in front of him, and if we stand on a high hill we shall get a view of him too.

poems.title: Book XI, 407
poems.author: Nicarchus
poems.text: As lean Menestratus was sitting in spring-time an ant came out and pulled him into a crevice; but a fly flew up and carried him off, just as the eagle carried Ganymede to the heavenly chamber of Zeus. He fell from the fly’s hands, but not even so did he light on the earth, but is hanging by his eyelids from a spider's web.
